extracted.intended_audience: TeX users / mathematical typists / authors of mathematical documents using plain TeX
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and low-level rules for producing high-quality mathematical typesetting with plain TeX: punctuation placement, font and spacing conventions, math glue, delimiters, atom/list structure, and macro usage. Aimed at authors and macro-writers who prepare mathematical manuscripts in TeX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation placement for inline vs displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: When a formula is in the text (inline), put the punctuation mark after the closing $; when the formula is displayed, put the punctuation before the $$.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If $x<0$, we have shown that $$y=f(x).$$ Rationale: TeX's paragraph spacing works best when sentence punctuation is not treated as part of the formula. Avoid typing punctuation that belongs to the sentence inside the $...$ for inline formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep sentence punctuation outside inline math when punctuation belongs to sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a comma/period/other punctuation belongs linguistically to the sentence rather than to the formula, leave it outside the $'s; conversely keep punctuation inside $'s if it truly belongs to the formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: for $x = a, b$, or $c$ (bad) — instead write for $x=a$, $b$, or $c$, or better: for $x=a$, or $c$. Reason: TeX treats a whole expression inside $ as a single formula and spacing/line-break behaviour will differ (thin spaces inside formula vs normal interword spaces outside). Also formula-internal commas usually prevent line breaks at undesired places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \mathsurround to add space around inline formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX inserts extra space before and after each formula via the \mathsurround parameter; plain TeX sets \mathsurround=0pt by default.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want a bit of visual separation around inline formulas (as some typists do), set \mathsurround to a nonzero value (e.g. 1pt). The value in force when TeX reads the closing $ is used at both sides of the formula. Note extra space might disappear into margins at line start/end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set common mathematical functions in roman type
rubrics_metrics.description: Common functions (log, sin, cos, exp, lim, max, etc.) should be set in roman type, not italic, and with appropriate spacing: plain TeX provides 32 control sequences for these (e.g. \sin, \log, \lim, \max, \Pr).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$, $\lim_{x\to0}{\sin x\over x}=1$. If a needed function is not provided, define a control sequence modeled on Appendix B or use {\rm ...} or \hbox{...} with caveats (see \hbox vs \rm). Note that some are treated as large operators (limits behave differently in display style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish \bmod (binary) and \pmod (parenthesized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \bmod when 'mod' is a binary operator (between two quantities); use \pmod when 'mod' occurs parenthetically at the end of a formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: \pmod inserts its own parentheses; the quantity after \pmod should be braced if it is not a single token. Example: $x\equiv y+1\pmod{m^2}$ vs $\gcd(m,n)=\gcd(n,m\bmod n)$.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use roman type for physical units separated by a thin space
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical units appearing in formulas should be set in roman type and separated from preceding material by a thin space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $55\rm\,mi/hr$, $g=9.8\rm\,m/sec^2$, $1\,m=1.000028\,cc$. The thin space prevents visual clumping between number and unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insert a thin space before differentials (\,dx)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas involving integrals and differentials look best when a thin space appears before the differential (e.g. \; or \, before dx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \int_{-\infty}^0 f(x)\,dx, $y\,dx-x\,dy$, $dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta$. Note exceptions: when dt appears alone in a fraction numerator, extra \,'s are unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insert thin space after factorials when next token is letter/number/opening delimiter
rubrics_metrics.description: After a factorial symbol '!' you should insert a thin space if the next character is a letter, digit, or opening delimiter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $(2n)!/\bigl(n!\,(n+1)!\bigr)$ and $${52!\over13!\,13!\,26!}$$. This prevents cramped appearance such as between '!' and following letter/delimiter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate adjacent formulas in text by words, not just commas; otherwise add interword space
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sentence would place two formulas next to each other, prefer to use words to separate them; if not, insert additional interword space explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: The Fibonacci numbers satisfy $F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}, n\ge2$. Better: $F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}$, \; for $n\ge2$ or insert backslash-space or \quad/\u to add visual separation. Example offered: ... $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$, \ $n\ge2$. (Use a visible separation to compensate for missing words.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \quad and \qquad to control horizontal spacing in displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \quad (one em) and \qquad (two ems) to insert printer's quad spacing, commonly used to separate equation and side condition in displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example recommended: $$F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2},\qquad n\ge2.$$ Note: \quad in plain TeX is an abbreviation for \hskip1em\relax and its width is taken from the current text font (so it is independent of math size/style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on TeX's automatic thin/medium/thick spacing but use \,, \>, \;, \! sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX automatically inserts thin, medium and thick spaces in formulas; the explicit commands are \, (thin), \> (medium), \; (thick), and \! (negative thin). These are normally used rarely to correct local optical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical nominal sizes: thin = 3mu, medium = 4mu plus/stretch minus, thick = 5mu plus/stretch (mu units). Use these only after you see proofs and need fine tuning (examples: \sqrt2\,x, \sqrt{\,\log x}, n/\!\log n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding and using mu glue: \mskip, \mkern, and mu units
rubrics_metrics.description: Math glue uses 'mu' units (math units). Use \mskip{<muglue>} and \mkern<mu> for glue/kern in math; conversely \hskip/\kern must not take mu units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \mskip 9mu plus 2mu inserts half an em with stretch. Appendix B defines \thinmuskip, \medmuskip, \thickmuskip. There are 18mu to an em (em taken from family 2). TeX insists on using mu for \mskip/\mkern; using \hskip/\kern with mu is incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \mskip/\mkern vs \hskip/\kern appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \mskip and \mkern when you need math glue/kern in mu units (and when spacing should scale with math size); use \hskip and \kern for ordinary horizontal spaces (pt/em) and never give them mu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: \mkern18mu gives one em of horizontal space in current math size; \mskip uses muskip values (can include stretch/shrink) whereas \hskip uses regular units. This preserves correct scaling in subscripts/scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of \hbox in math: font and sizing caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: \hbox{...} can be used to get roman letters into formulas because its contents are processed in horizontal mode where spaces are significant, but the box uses the current text font and the box has fixed size behavior (doesn't scale for subscripts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $\sqrt{\hbox{Var}(X)}$ works; but in a slanted theorem environment \hbox may produce slanted text unless you explicitly use \rm inside the \hbox: $\sqrt{\hbox{\rm Var}(X)}$. Also \hbox contents are typeset in same size regardless of subscript level (unlike proper math fonts), so prefer \rm or specific math font macros when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \rm / \bf / \cal / \mit / \it appropriately and know their scopes/limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Font switches in math affect limited character sets: \rm and \bf affect only A–Z, a–z, digits 0–9, uppercase Greek and math accents; \cal works only on uppercase letters A–Z; \mit is 'math italic' (affects uppercase Greek), \it is 'text italic'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: $\bf a+b=\Phi_m$ — only letters/digits/upper Greek are changed, punctuation and many symbols remain unchanged. Avoid applying \cal to lowercase or Greek letters (weird results). Use \mit to change uppercase Greek; math accents should not be used when \mit is in effect (math italic font usually has no accents). Font changes are grouped by $...$ so they are local to the formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \it (text italic) in math for literal italic words or multi-letter identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \it inside math mode if you need an actual italic word (not math-italic spacing) or when typesetting multi-letter identifiers (programmer identifiers) so ligatures and underlines behave as intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $\it last:=first$ and $\it x\_coord(point\_2)$. Math italic letters are wider and spacing differs; for actual italic words use \it to get correct appearance and ligatures (e.g. 'fi'). Note \it is text italic and available only at text size—avoid in subscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the structure of math lists and atoms (nucleus, superscript, subscript; atom types)
rubrics_metrics.description: A math list is composed of items, the most important of which are atoms; each atom has a nucleus, a superscript field, and a subscript field. There are thirteen atom kinds (Ord, Op, Bin, Rel, Open, Close, Punct, Inner, Over, Under, Accent, Rad, Vcenter) with specific behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can inspect representation with \showlists in math mode. Example interpretations: Ord is ordinary atom like x, Op is large operator like \sum, Bin is binary like '+', Rel is relation like '=', Open is '(', Close is ')', etc. Some atoms carry extra info (Op atoms may be marked \limits or \nolimits; Rad atoms contain a delimiter field; Accent atoms contain family/char codes). This knowledge helps in macro-writing and diagnosing spacing/formatting issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delimiters and \delimiter numeric conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Delimiters can be specified numerically via \delimiter <number> where the number encodes class and small/large variant positions; when \delimiter follows \left or \right the class digit is ignored, and when used elsewhere it drops the three rightmost digits and acts as a \mathchar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \def\langle{\delimiter 11 426830A} meaning \langle is opening (class 4) with small variant "268 and large "30A. If a delimiter's decode is negative it causes an error; TeX first tries the small variant then the large when searching for a suitable delimiter. These numeric conventions pack lots of information and are useful for low-level format definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: \radical and \mathaccent usage for square roots and accents
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX implements square root signs and math accents via \radical (followed by a delimiter code) and \mathaccent (followed by a math character code); common macros like \sqrt and \widehat are defined in terms of these primitives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example definitions: \def\sqrt{\radical 11 270370} and \def\widehat{\mathaccent 11 362}. TeX uses the family and character positions to position the radical/accent; Appendix G gives precise positioning. By changing definitions and having appropriate font glyphs, TeX can be extended to typeset different radical signs and accent symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fonts/families assignment conventions (family 1 italics, 2 symbols, 3 large symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX conventionally uses family 1 for math italic letters, family 2 for ordinary math symbols, and family 3 for large symbols; families 2 and 3 must have special \fontdimen parameters that govern math spacing (cmsy and cmex supply these).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INITEX initializes mathcodes so letters A–Z, a–z are class 7 family 1, digits 0–9 class 7 family 0. Other families can be reassigned; \newfam allocates symbolic names to families. You can modify fontdimen via \fontdimen to adjust spacing, but assigning cmsy/cmex to families 2 and 3 is almost mandatory for correct math spacing.
